<noinclude><pagequality level="2" user="Amire80" />{{GHGcorrected}}<!-- This page is mostly proofread, however it cannot be finalized because the Babylonian vowel marks are not in Unicode and cannot be written. Perhaps they can be entered as images. --></noinclude><section begin="par8" />{{GHGmargin-letter|8|d}}
The names of the vowels are mostly taken from the form and action of the mouth in producing the various sounds, as {{GHGheb|text=פַּ֫תַח|translate=opening}}; {{GHGheb|text=צֵ֫רֵי|translate=a wide parting}} (of the mouth), also {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫בֶר}} (={{GHGpron|ĭ}}) {{GHGtranslate|breaking}}, {{GHGtranslate|parting}} (cf. the Arab, {{GHGpron|kasr}}); {{GHGheb|text=חִ֫ירֶק}} (also {{GHGheb|text=חִרֶק}}) {{GHGtranslate|narrow opening}}; {{GHGheb|text=ח֫וֹלֶם|translate=closing}}, according to others {{GHGtranslate|fullness}}, i.e. of the mouth (also {{GHGheb|text=מְלֹא פּוּם}}<ref>On the erroneous use of the term {{GHGpron|melo pum}}, only in Germany, for {{GHGterm|šûreq}} (hence also pronounced {{GHGpron|melu pum}} to indicate {{GHGpron|û}}), see {{nowrap|E. Nestle}}, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1904, p. 597 ff.; Bacher, ibid., p. 799 ff., Melopum; Simonsen, ibid., p. 807 ff.</ref> {{GHGtranslate|fullness of the mouth}}). {{GHGheb|text=קָ֫מֶץ}}<ref>The usual spelling {{GHGheb|text=קָמֶץ}} and {{GHGheb|text=פַּתַח}} takes the words certainly rightly as Hebrew substantives; according to De Lagarde ({{GHGcite|title=Gött. gel. Anz.}} 1886, p. 873, and so previously Luzzatto), {{GHGheb|text=קָמֵץ}} and {{GHGheb|text=פָתַח}} are rather Aram. participles, like {{GHGterm|Dageš}}, &c., and consequently to be transliterated <!-- no GHGtranslit here - unusual spellings -->{{GHGpron|Qâmēṣ}} and {{GHGpron|Pâthaḥ}}.</ref> also denotes a slighter, as {{GHGheb|text=שׁוּרֶק}} and {{GHGheb|text=קִבּוּץ}} (also {{GHGheb|text=קבוץ פּוּם}}) a firmer, compression or contraction of the mouth. {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>gôl}} ({{GHGheb|text=סְגוֹל|translate=bunch of grapes}}) takes its name from its form. So {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלֹשׁ נְקֻדּוֹת}} ({{GHGtranslate|three points}}) is another name for Qibbûṣ.

{{GHGmargin-letter|8|e}}
Moreover the names were mostly so formed (but only later), that the sound of each vowel is heard in the first syllable ({{GHGheb|text=קָמֶץ}} for {{GHGheb|text=קֹמֶץ}}, {{GHGheb|text=פַּתַח}} for {{GHGheb|text=פֶּתַח}}, {{GHGheb|text=צֵרִי}} for {{GHGheb|text=צְרִי}}); in order to carry this out consistently some even write {{GHGpron|Sägôl}}, {{GHGpron|Qomeṣ-ḥatûf}}, {{GHGpron|Qübbûṣ}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|8|f}}
'''2.''' As the above examples show, the vowel sign stands regularly ''under'' the consonant, ''after'' which it is to be pronounced, {{GHGheb|text=רָ|pron=rā}}, {{GHGheb|text=רַ|pron=ră}}, {{GHGheb|text=רֵ|pron=rē}}, {{GHGheb|text=רֻ|pron=rŭ}}, &c. The {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} called {{GHGterm|furtivum|en=furtive, stolen}} ({{GHGpar|22|f}}) alone forms an exception to this rule, being pronounced before the consonant, {{GHGheb|text=רוּחַ}} {{GHGpron|rû<sup>a</sup>ḥ}} (wind, spirit). The {{GHGpron|Ḥōlĕm}} (without {{GHGpron|wāw}}) stands on the left above the consonant; {{GHGheb|text=רֹ|pron=rō}} (but {{GHGheb|text=לֹ|pron=lō}}). If {{GHGheb|text=א}}, as a vowel letter, follows a consonant which is to be pronounced with {{GHGpron|ō}}, the point is placed over its right arm, thus {{GHGheb|text=בֹא}}, {{GHGheb|text=רֹאשׁ}}; but e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בֹאָם}}, since {{GHGheb|text=א}} here begins a syllable.

{{GHGmargin-letter|8|g}}
<small>
No dot is used for the Ḥolem when {{GHGpron|ō}} (of course without {{GHGterm|wāw}}) is pronounced after {{GHGpron|śîn}} or before {{GHGpron|šîn}}. Hence {{GHGheb|text=שׂנֵא|translate=śônē}} (hating), {{GHGheb|text=נְשׂא|pron=n<sup>e</sup>śō}} (to bear), {{GHGheb|text=משֶׁה|translate=môšè}} (not {{GHGheb|text=מֹשֶׁה}}); but {{GHGheb|text=שֹׁמֵר|translate=šômēr}} (a watchman). When {{GHGpron|ō}} precedes the {{GHGpron|śîn}}, the dot is placed over its right arm, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יִרְפּשֹׁ|translate=yirpōś}} (he treads with the feet), {{GHGheb|text=הַנּֽשְֹׁאִים|pron=hannôś<sup>e</sup>ʾîm}} (those who carry).</small>

<small>In the sign {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}}, the {{GHGheb|text=ו}} may also be a consonant. The {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} is then either to be read {{GHGpron|ōw}} (necessarily so when a consonant otherwise without a vowel precedes, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לֹוֶה|translate=lôwè}}, lending) or {{GHGpron|wō}}, when a vowel already precedes the {{GHGheb|text=ו}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עָוֹן|pron=ʿāwôn}} (iniquity) for {{GHGheb|text=עָווֹן}}. In more exact printing, a distinction is at least made between {{GHGheb|text=וֹ|translate=wo}} and {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} (i.e. either {{GHGpron|ô}} or, when another vowel follows the {{GHGterm|wāw}}, {{GHGpron|ôw}}<ref>Since 1846 we have become acquainted with a system of vocalization different in many respects from the common method. The vowel signs, all except {{GHGheb|text=וּ}}, are there placed ''above'' the consonants, and differ almost throughout in form, and some even as regards the sound which they denote: {Babylonian â/ā mark} = {{GHGpron|â}}, {{GHGpron|ā}}, {Babylonian ă/è mark} = tone-bearing {{GHGpron|ă}} and {{GHGpron|è}}, {Babylonian ê/ē mark} = {{GHGpron|ê}}, {{GHGpron|ē}}, {Babylonian î mark} = {{GHGpron|î}}, {Babylonian ô/ō mark} = {{GHGpron|ô}}, {{GHGpron|ō}}, {Babylonian û mark} = {{GHGpron|û}}. In an unsharpened syllable {Babylonian toneless ă/è mark} = toneless {{GHGpron|ă}} and {{GHGpron|è}}, and also Ḥaṭeph Pathaḥ; {Babylonian toneless ĕ mark} = toneless {{GHGpron|ĕ}} and Ḥaṭeph S<sup>e</sup>ghôl; {Babylonian ĭ mark} = {{GHGpron|ĭ}}, {Babylonian ŭ mark} = {{GHGpron|ŭ}}, {Babylonian ŏ mark} = {{GHGpron|ŏ}}, and Ḥaṭeph Qameṣ. Lastly in toneless syllables before Dageš, {Babylonian ă mark} = {{GHGpron|ă}}, {Babylonian ĕ mark} = {{GHGpron|ĕ}}, {Babylonian i mark} = {{GHGpron|i}}, {Babylonian ŭ mark} = {{GHGpron|ŭ}}, {Babylonian {{GHGtranslit|a-ring-brev}} mark} = {{GHGpron|{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-brev}}}}. Š<sup>e</sup>wâ is {Babylonian Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mark}. The accents differ less and stand in some cases under the line of the consonants. Besides this complicated system of the Codex Babylonicus (see below) and other MSS., there is a simpler one, used in Targums. It is still uncertain whether the latter is the foundation of the former (as Merx, {{GHGcite|title=Chrest. Targ.}} xi, and Bacher, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1895, p. 15 ff.), or is a later development of it among the Jews of South Arabia (as Praetorius, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1899, p. 181 ff.). For the older literature on this {{GHGterm|Babylonian punctuation}} ({{GHGheb|text=נִקּוּד בַּבְלִי}}), as it is called, see A. Harkavy and H. L. Strack, {{GHGcite|title=Katalog der hebr. Bibelhandschr. der Kaiserl. öffentl. Bibliothek zu St. Petersb.}}, St. Petersb. and Lpz., 1875, parts i and ii, p. 223 ff. A more thorough study of the system was made possible by H. Strack’s facsimile edition of the {{GHGcite|title=Prophetarum posteriorum codex Babylonicus Petropolitanus}} (St. Petersb., 1876, la. fol.) of the year 916, which Firkowitsch discovered in 1839, in the synagogue at Tschufutkale in the Crimea. The MS. has been shown by Ginsburg ({{GHGcite|title=Recueil des travaux rédigés en mémoire... de Chwolson}}, Berlin, 1899, p. 149, and {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}, pp. 216 ff., 475 f.) to contain a recension of the Biblical text partly Babylonian and partly Palestinian; cf. also Barnstein, {{GHGcite|title=The Targum of Onkelos to Genesis}}, London, 1896, p. 6 f. Strack edited a fragment of it in {{GHGcite|title=Hosea et Joel prophetae ad fidem cod. Babylon. Petrop.}}, St. Petersb. 1875. Cf. also the publication by A. Merx, quoted above, {{GHGpar|7|h}}, and his {{GHGcite|title=Chrestomathia Targumica}}, Berlin, 1888; G. Margoliouth, in the {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|PSBA.|Proceedings of the Society of Biblical Archæology. London, 1879 ff.}}}} xv. 4, and M. Gaster, ibid.; P. Kahle, {{GHGcite|title=Der masoret. Text des A.T. nach d. Überlief. der babyl. Juden}}, Lpz. 1902, with the valuable review by Rahlfs in {{GHGcite|title=GGA}}. 1903, no. 5; Nestle, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1905, p. 719 (Babylonian {Babylonian ă/è mark} = {{GHGheb|text=ע}}. According to the opinion formerly prevailing, this Babylonian punctuation exhibits the system which was developed in the Eastern schools, corresponding to and contemporaneous with the Western or Tiberian system, although a higher degree of originality, or approximation to the original of both systems of punctuation, was generally conceded to the latter. Recently, however, Wickes, {{GHGcite|title=Accents of the Twenty-one Books}}, Oxford, 1887, p. 142 ff, has endeavoured to show, from the accents, that the ‘Babylonian’ punctuation may certainly be ''an'' Oriental, but is by no means ''the'' Oriental system. It is rather to be regarded, according to him, as a later and not altogether successful attempt to modify, and thus to simplify, the system common to all the Schools in the East and West. Strack, {{GHGcite|title=Wiss. Jahresb. der {{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1879, p. 124, established the probability that the vowels of the superlinear punctuation arose under ''Arab'' influence from the vowel letters {{GHGheb|text=יוא}} (so previously Pinsker and Graetz), while the Tiberian system shows ''Syrian'' influence.
<br />
A third, widely different system (Palestinian), probably the basis of the other two, is described by A. Neubauer, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|JQR.|Jewish Quarterly Review.}}}} vii. 1895, p. 361 ff., and Friedländer, ibid., p. 564 ff., and {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|PSBA.|Proceedings of the Society of Biblical Archæology. London, 1879 ff.}}}} 1896, p. 86 ff.; C. Levias, {{GHGcite|title=Journ. of Sem. Lang. and Lit.}}, xv. p. 157 ff.; and esp. P. Kahle, ‘Beitr. zu der Gesch. der hebr. Punktation,’ and in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1901, p. 273 ff. and in {{GHGcite|title=Der masoret. Text des A.T.}} (see above), chiefly dealing with the Berlin MS. Or. qu. 680, which contains a number of variants on the biblical text, and frequently agrees with the transcriptions of the LXX and Jerome.</ref>).
</small>
